FACDEV.TITLE: Designing Curriculum for Working PAs: Asynchronous/Hybrid Models & the Adult Learner
FACDEV.DESC:
This webinar is for programs considering developing a doctoral program. Experienced program directors will share lessons learned from developing and refining post-professional doctoral programs, highlighting approaches that foster academic success, learner engagement, and program quality. Participants will gain practical perspectives on designing educational experiences that meet the needs of today’s learners while supporting institutional goals and program growth.
By the end of this session, participants will be able to:
Evaluate asynchronous and hybrid curriculum designs suited to full-time working PA clinicians.
Compare scholarly-project models (publication-focused vs. QI/applied project) and their advising structures.
Identify strategies to engage and retain and support adult learners balancing clinical work with study.

FACDEV.TITLE: Strategies for Retaining PA Students with Disabilities
FACDEV.DESC: PA programs are seeing increasing numbers of students with disabilities entering healthcare education, but many programs still struggle with how to effectively support, accommodate, and retain these learners. In this webinar, Jon McGough, MEd will share strategies for PA programs on how to create more accessible learning environments while maintaining academic and clinical standards. Participants will explore common barriers faced by students with disabilities in PA education, gain clarity on legal and ethical responsibilities surrounding accommodations, and learn how proactive support practices can improve retention rates and overall program outcomes. The webinar will also address best practices for communication, documentation, and fostering a culture of inclusion within PA programs.

FACDEV.TITLE: One Year Later: Updates and Considerations for PA Program Leadership
FACDEV.DESC: As the higher education landscape continues to shift, PA programs are increasingly challenged to balance advocacy for their programs with alignment to institutional priorities, and evolving state and federal policy requirements. Program leaders navigate complex institutional structures, engage effectively with university leadership, and understand the legal considerations that can influence program operations and strategic decision-making. Jason Qu, an attorney with extensive experience in healthcare and higher education law, will discuss how PA program leaders can approach these challenges with greater clarity and confidence. Qu will outline the types of conversations programs should be having with institutional leaders and legal counsel and highlight common legal and policy issues affecting PA education. Qu will be joined in conversation by Emma Sellers, PAEA’s Chief of Recruitment and Engagement, for a timely discussion about the broader higher education environment and what it means for PA programs today. Together, they will explore emerging pressures facing programs, offer context for recent developments in policy and governance, and provide actionable strategies to help program leaders make informed, proactive decisions. What you’ll learn 1. Key legal and policy considerations currently affecting PA education 2. Approaches for engaging institutional counsel and leadership in productive, strategic conversations, and 3. Practical strategies for advocating for your program while aligning with broader institutional goals

FACDEV.ORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

This session will focus on tips for spotting and dealing with AI hallucinations, inaccuracies, and other “made-up” facts, particularly as they relate to citations in scholarly work. FACDEV.TITLE: PAEA South Regional Education Meeting
Prompt Like a Pro: AI Prompt Engineering to Create High-Quality Instructional Materials
FACDEV.ORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
FACDEV.DESC:
This session equips faculty with practical skills to optimize AI prompts for generating high-quality instructional materials. Student Impact: Well-engineered prompts yield clearer assignments, better-scaffolded learning progressions, and more effective formative assessments—directly supporting student engagement and success. Faculty who streamline materials development through AI also reclaim time for high-impact mentoring and feedback.
Faculty Impact: By analyzing what makes prompts effective, participants develop metacognitive awareness about instructional clarity that transfers beyond AI use. The iterative refinement process models reflective practice, while grounding techniques in cognitive psychology (cognitive load theory, transfer of learning) reinforces evidence-informed teaching. Faculty gain both immediate efficiency and deeper pedagogical insight, fostering ongoing growth in teaching development.

Clinical Accommodations in PA Education: What You Should Know
FACDEV.DESC: While classroom-based accommodations are widely recognized and routinely implemented, clinical accommodations have only recently begun to receive meaningful attention. Emerging research documents the significant barriers students encounter in clinical education and the downstream consequences of inadequate access—including compromised well-being, lower board performance, and delayed graduation. This training focused on addressing reasonable clinical accommodations, evidence-based accommodation strategies to address barriers, and effective communication practices for collaaborating with clinical partners.

FACDEV.TITLE: Build Your Own Course chatbots-It's Easy
FACDEV.ORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
FACDEV.DESC: In this workshop, you will learn to design, build, and ethically integrate custom AI chatbots into your courses, while exploring practical insights and best practices.   As a takeaway, you will build your own Informational Chatbot that answers student questions about course policies, requirements, assignments, and deadlines. You will also be introduced to two additional chatbot models you can build using the same design principles: a Tutor Chatbot for supporting content mastery, and a Grammar Editing Chatbot for assignment-specific writing feedback. Together, these custom GPTs make it easier to support students’ learning and course engagement while modeling responsible AI use in your classes.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Expanding and Enhancing Physician Assistant Education
Primary Care Training and Enhancement: Expanding and Enhancing Physician Assistant Education
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Primary Care Training and Enhancement: Expanding and Enhancing Physician Assistant Education
Primary Care Training and Enhancement: Physician Assistant Program HRSA-19-087
University of Texas Rio Grande Valley-Department of Physician Assistant
Frank Ambriz, Department Chair, Associate Professor and Project Director
956-665-7072, frank.ambriz@utrgv.edu
Funding Preference: High rate MUC graduate placement
Abstract:
Laredo, Texas located in Webb county is just 150 miles (two-and-a-half-mile drive) to the northwest up-river along the Texas-Mexico border from our UTRGV campus. Laredo is the second fasting growing metropolitan area in the country. The medical community of the Laredo area has reached out to our PA program in recruiting PAs to practice in Laredo to assist in serving the medical needs of this rapidly growing region. Webb County is a rural area with a population of over 90 percent Hispanic, with a third of its population in poverty including 40% of all children in the county and is a medically underserved community. UTRGV proposes to offer clinical training in Webb county to 50 or more PA students. Assign and training 50 physician assistant students to completing 150 clinical rotations clinical at Webb county sites. This will encourage participants, as shown in our track record of current graduates, to seek employment and practice in an area close to where they are trained.
Approximately 80 percent of Texas counties are designated Health Profession Shortage Areas for mental health. The Department of State Health Services has said that one-third of adults with serious and persistent mental illness receive the services they need, while the percentage is worse for children with severe emotional disturbance. Due to a chronic shortage of mental health providers, much of the burden of mental health care in rural
areas have shifted to the primary health care sector. Primary care clinicians, however, generally lack
training and time to provide proper mental health care. UTRGV proposes to enhance mental health education and training to 100 first year PA students, 80 second year PA students and another 80 capstone PA students.
The UTRGV Department of Physician Assistant is proposing to address and offer solutions to these concerns with this grant proposal. Specific objectives:
Objective I. Recruit and train physician assistant students to practice in the medically underserve Webb county communities.
Objective II. Enhance our existing PA psychiatry curriculum and Clinical training in Behavior and Mental Health to include opioid, MAT, and substance abuse.
Objective 3. Develop and implement an approach to improve PA students and faculty wellness.
The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley Physician Assistant program is in Edinburg, TX on the southern Texas-Mexico border and services four counties in the Rio Grande Valley of South Texas: Cameron, Hidalgo, Starr and Willacy counties. Over 50% of our graduates in the last three classes are currently working in medically underserved communities. Since the opening of our PA program, our graduates have transformed healthcare delivery in our region by practicing in the medically underserve communities where they have been trained.
UTRGV’s Department of Physician Assistant will be requesting Funding Preference base on high rate of graduates placed in a practice setting serving medically underserved communities (MUC). In the past two academic years, nd 55% of our graduates are practicing in medically underserved communities (MUC).

INTELLCONT.TITLE: The Voluntary Practice of Eugenics: Risk-Taking and Religiosity as Determinants of Attitudes Toward Conceiving Children with Potential Genetic Disorders and Inheritable Diseases
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: HSOA Journal of Physical Medicine, Rehabilitation, and Disabilities
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The purpose of this study was to examine attitudes toward the voluntary practice of eugenics among people with high-risk inheritable diseases and genetic disorders. Participants consisted of 426 students attending two large public universities in the south and southwestern regions of the United States. The study used the modified scale of attitudes toward mental retardation and eugenics, the risk-taking questionnaire, and the dimensions of religious ideology importance scale. A general linear model was tested to answer the research question. The results showed that the model was significant (p < 0.001; adjusted r2 of 0.078). Significant main effects were found in race [F (4,378) = 2.538, p = 0.04, η² = 0.026], risk avoidance [F (1,378) = 12.536, p < 0.001, η² = 0.032] and importance of religion [F (1,378) = 5.530, p = 0.019, η² = 0.014]. Cultural, ethnic, and religious variables influenced people’s views toward disability. One’s perception of both disability and its impact on quality of life will influence his or her feelings about eugenics and babies with congenital conditions.

PRESENT.TITLE: Impact of Late Admissions on Academic Performance in Physician Assistant Education
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: This study investigates the impact of late admissions on the academic performance of students in the physician assistant (PA) program at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), spanning the graduating cohorts from 2019 through 2024 (the 2024 cohort was included in partial analysis as it has not yet graduated). Late admissions criteria varied across cohorts, with the class of 2019 identifying late admits as those accepted from April 2017 onwards, and from 2020 to 2024, late admits were defined as applicants accepted from January onwards. This temporal benchmark was established by analyzing the distribution of offer letters and the completion of the majority of the class rosters.

PRESENT.TITLE: Diagnosing the Future: AI-Driven Clinical Scenarios in PA Education
PRESENT.ABSTRACT:
The purpose of exploring this topic is to showcase the innovative integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in both didactic and clinical phases of Physician Assistant (PA) education. By presenting our experiences and insights, we aim to demonstrate how AI technologies have revolutionized teaching and learning in PA programs. From dynamic classroom activities to efficient case creation for clinical assessments, AI offers transformative opportunities to enhance student engagement, critical thinking, and clinical proficiency. Through this poster, we seek to share our journey of harnessing AI to create immersive learning experiences, ultimately preparing PA students for success in real-world clinical practice.

PRESENT.TITLE: Effect of Study Methodology and Self-Efficacy on PACKRAT Scores
PRESENT.ABSTRACT:
Purpose: Effective study methods may vary but are required for college success specifically in intense programs like the physician assistant program. Individual versus group study methods have been under debate with some results more in favor of group study. This difference was not evaluated within physician assistant programs particularly after the application of team based learning method (TBL). The aim of this study is to evaluate study habits of PA students, their perceived benefits for each study method, their perceived self-efficacy for self-regulated learning and the association with their PACKRAT score.
Methods: An online survey was developed and sent to PA students assessing their study methods, personality type, and their perceived self-efficacy for self-regulated learning using Banadura’s self-efficacy scale. Descriptive and regression analyses were conducted using STATA 14.
Results: Respondents (N=54) were mainly females (74%), with a mean age of 30 (±6) years old and 35.8% reported being visual learners. Half of the respondents preferred to study individually while 3.7% preferred group study and 46.3% reported both individual and group study. 80% reported studying individually is effective when compared to only 50% reporting group study is effective. Respondents were 75% -85% confident regarding their self-regulated learning methods used and 43.4% used repetition as their method of memorization technique. Mean Packrat score was 146.8 (±18.4, range 102- 195). Mean Packrat score was not significantly different by study methodology. Additionally there was no significant correlation between Packrat scores and any of the self-efficacy measures. Simple and adjusted linear regression did not reveal any significant relationship between study methodology and Packrat score.
Discussion: Though the study did not reveal any significant relationship between study methodology, perceived self-efficacy for self-regulated learning and the PACKRAT score yet this can be attributed to the small sample size. A similar study is needed across various PA programs in order to increase the study sample size.
